data.note: Third-party protocols that impose no ceiling of their own and pass whatever the endpoint accepts: Roon RAAT, the reference implementation's network audio adapter, Ravenna and AES67. policy._bits_above_hz: "unknown" rather than absent, and the difference is deliberate. PGGB's DAC-settings guide, read 2026-11-23, states that at 32fS a USB driver may limit playback to 16 bits. That is somebody else's claim about hardware this catalogue has not identified, so it is not recorded as a figure - recording it would make the engine assert a truncation at a rate nobody here has checked, and a wrong record is worse than no record. What it does earn is this field being a live question instead of silence. The bench item is one sweep per driver: ask for 24 bits at 1.4112 MHz and read back the word width the device actually receives.

open_doubt.text: This is not a standalone converter. Accuphase's own page describes the DAC-50 as an OPTION BOARD that installs in a rear slot of a supported component, so the device a listener actually owns is the host amplifier or player, and that is what the driver will name. The record is kept because its chip-level facts hold, but it cannot be matched by a model name a listener would recognise, and its inputs belong to the host. The inverse of the RME and Schiit case: there a model name covered several devices, here a model name is a part of one.

data._corrected: This record was called "Yggdrasil" and carried a quote about ONE of its three variants. Schiit sells the Yggdrasil in three flavours on three different converters: the OG on Analog Devices AD5791 at 20 bits, Less is More on four TI DAC8812 at 16 bits, and More is Less on TI DAC11001 at 20 bits. Only the second is described here, and only the second is 16-bit - so the record's bits, its chip and its family were right for a device its own name did not identify. Renamed rather than generalised. The apparent contradiction between "16-bit TI DAC" and the ladder family was never one: all three are multibit ladder parts rather than delta-sigma, which is the whole point of Schiit's multibit line.
